name: Resiliparse, part of the ChatNoir Resiliparse toolkit (chatnoir-eu/chatnoir-resiliparse) from the Webis Group / Bauhaus-Universitaet Weimar and Leipzig. Ships alongside FastWARC in the same repository. The relevant entry point is `resiliparse.extract.html2text.extract_plain_text`. Sometimes referred to simply as 'the ChatNoir extractor' or 'the DCLM extractor'.
kind: Library -- a C/C++/Cython toolkit with Python bindings (a Rust port is in progress and explicitly not yet a stable crate), built on the Lexbor HTML engine. Comprises four subsystems: Parsing Utilities, Extraction Utilities, Process Guards, and Itertools.
maturity: Production, and production at a scale nothing else in this batch matches. It is the extractor behind DCLM-Baseline and is used in Dolma; it processes Common Crawl-scale corpora routinely. Version line 0.16.x, actively maintained by an academic group with an institutional stake (ChatNoir search engine) rather than a single hobbyist. The Rust port is prototype-grade and should not be counted as available.
license: Apache-2.0 for both Resiliparse and FastWARC. Permits use here without restriction, including redistribution and modification. Lexbor underneath is Apache-2.0 as well, so the whole stack is permissive.
keeps_and_discards: Two distinct modes, and the distinction matters more than the algorithm. With `main_content=False` (the default), `extract_plain_text` is not a content extractor at all -- it is a visible-text serializer: it walks the body, skips script/style/template, skips elements it judges hidden, and emits the text nodes. That mode is close to what this project actually needs and is routinely overlooked because everyone benchmarks the other one. With `main_content=True` it additionally applies a rule set that removes navigation blocks, sidebars, footers and similar boilerplate containers. Around this sits an unusually rich set of explicit toggles that no other extractor in this batch exposes: `alt_texts` (image alt text, on by default), `links` (emit href targets), `form_fields` (emit form input values and placeholders), `noscript`, `comments` (on by default), `post_meta` (on by default), `list_bullets`, `hidden_elements` (off by default), and `preserve_formatting` with three settings -- True for ASCII layout formatting, False for compact, and 'minimal_html' which retains structural markup. The toggle surface, not the heuristic, is the reusable idea: it makes the keep/discard decision a caller policy rather than a baked-in opinion.
structure_preserved: Configurable across a wider range than any peer. At `preserve_formatting=False` the output is a flat token stream with structure gone. At True it inserts ASCII layout -- blank lines between blocks, indentation, list bullets -- so nesting and ordering are recoverable by convention rather than by markup, which is close to the ASCII-wireframe idea this project already uses and is worth studying as prior art for exactly that. At 'minimal_html' it retains a reduced structural markup set, preserving nesting and tabular relations as real elements. What never survives in any mode: element identity, attributes other than the ones the toggles surface (href, alt, form values), the ancestor chain above kept content in main_content mode, and any relation between kept and discarded material. Shadow boundaries do not exist in its model -- it consumes serialized HTML into a Lexbor light DOM, so open shadow roots are absent unless pre-composed, closed roots are unrepresentable, and there is no unreachable marker either way.
interactive_elements: This is Resiliparse's one genuine differentiator in this batch: `form_fields=True` extracts form input values and placeholders, and `links=True` emits href targets. It is the only mainstream extractor here that treats controls as content worth surfacing rather than as noise to delete. But be precise about what it gives you -- it surfaces the VALUES and PLACEHOLDERS as text, not the controls as addressable affordances. There is no element type in the output, no name/id, no association between a label and its input, no form grouping, and no way to act on what was emitted. It is affordance-aware, not affordance-preserving. For this project it is the closest existing thing to 'tag plus interactivity' and simultaneously a demonstration of how far short surfacing-as-text falls.
interactive_state_fidelity: Near zero even with `form_fields=True`. A checkbox's checked state, an option's selected state, a control's disabled state, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-current and role are not emitted -- the toggle surfaces value and placeholder text only. aria attributes are consulted only in the negative direction, as part of the hidden-element decision. So the token cost of interactive state is again zero, and the affordance-state count is again zero, but Resiliparse is the one tool where the gap is a design choice with a visible seam rather than an absence: the toggle exists, the state axis simply was not carried through it. That makes it the right control for measuring what 'tag plus interactivity' actually costs -- run it with form_fields on and links on, and the delta between its token count and the fold's token count is the price of carrying state and address, isolated from the price of carrying the control at all.
layout_awareness: No geometry, no rendering, no computed style cascade -- and this is a stated design property, since it is built to run over WARC archives at Common Crawl scale where rendering is impossible by budget. Its hidden-element decision is attribute-local: inline `style` matched for display:none / visibility:hidden, the `hidden` attribute, and aria-hidden, exposed to the caller as `hidden_elements` (excluded by default). It does not parse or apply external stylesheets. [uncertain] on whether recent versions consult any additional style signals; the documentation does not enumerate the predicate and I could not verify the source. Net: satisfies no_layout_in_the_fold cleanly and inherits the corresponding blindness to CSS-driven concealment.
javascript_required: No, and by design it cannot use it. Resiliparse is a static-HTML pipeline aimed at archived bytes; client-rendered pages yield whatever the server sent, which for an SPA is a shell. It fires no scripts, requests no subresources, and sends no beacons during extraction, so reading is telemetry-free -- but in this project's architecture the browser has already executed the page before the fold runs, so that property buys nothing and the SPA blindness is pure cost. Its relevance here is as a post-hoc processor of an already-captured serialization, not as a live-page reader.
evaluation_method: Three separate evidence lines, with different oracles. (1) Bevendorff, Gupta, Kiesel and Stein, 'An Empirical Comparison of Web Content Extraction Algorithms', SIGIR 2023 -- a reproducibility study that unifies EIGHT prior extraction datasets into a common format and scores extractors with ROUGE-LSum and Levenshtein distance against reference texts, plus a per-page extraction-complexity estimate used as a difficulty proxy. Sequence-based metrics, so unlike WCXB's word bags this one does score ordering. (2) WCXB (arXiv 2605.21097), word-bag F1 over 1,497 development pages, plus the with-snippet-recall / without-snippet-inclusion pair. (3) DCLM (DataComp-LM), which is a fundamentally different and more interesting method: extractors are swapped inside a fixed pretraining pipeline and judged by the DOWNSTREAM benchmark scores of the models trained on their output. That is an outcome oracle, not an agreement oracle.
corpus_size_and_origins: SIGIR 2023: eight pre-existing datasets merged, which inherits all of their reach problems at once -- CleanEval's 2006-2007 pages, L3S-GN1's 621 Google News pages from 2010, Dragnet, and similar -- so the aggregate is large but its median page predates responsive layout, consent banners and shadow DOM, and no single origin count is meaningful across the merge. WCXB: 2,008 pages, 1,613 domains, September 2025 to March 2026, predominantly English, static snapshots with SPAs explicitly excluded, CC-BY-4.0. DCLM: Common Crawl at trillions of tokens, effectively unbounded in origin count and genuinely web-scale, but with no per-page ground truth at all -- the corpus is enormous and the annotation is nil. Note the pattern across all three: no corpus here contains a live page, a rendered SPA, a consent-gated capture, or a shadow-DOM component, so none of them samples the population this project's 136 live pages are drawn from.
reported_precision_recall: WCXB dev set, word-bag F1: Resiliparse 0.797, placing third behind rs-trafilatura 0.859 and MinerU-HTML 0.827, and ahead of Trafilatura 0.791, dom-smoothie 0.762, ReaderLM-v2 0.741, BoilerPy3 0.687, Readability 0.674. The informative decomposition is the snippet pair: Resiliparse retains 74.5% of ground-truth content while admitting 22.8% boilerplate, against Trafilatura's 69.5% / 6.6%. So Resiliparse buys +5 points of recall for +16 points of contamination -- a distinctly high-recall, low-precision profile, and the only tool in the batch whose bias runs the direction this project's capture-first posture wants. DCLM reports that Resiliparse-extracted training data improves Core benchmark scores by roughly 2.5 points over Common Crawl WET files, that Trafilatura achieves similar downstream quality, and that Resiliparse is about 8x faster -- which is why DCLM-Baseline uses it. Parsing throughput: roughly 1,150 documents/second on a title-extraction benchmark over 42,015 documents. I could not retrieve the SIGIR 2023 numeric table directly (the ACM PDF returns 403), so the ROUGE-LSum figures are [uncertain] here.
independent_oracle: The strongest position in this batch, though still not clean. Its three evidence lines do not share an oracle: SIGIR 2023 scores sequence agreement with human reference texts, WCXB scores word-bag agreement with an LLM-drafted human-adjudicated span, and DCLM scores downstream language-model benchmark performance with no reference text at all. That third one is a genuinely independent oracle in the sense this field asks for -- it shares no assumption with the extractor, does not presuppose that a page has one contiguous main content, and can in principle rank an extractor that a span-agreement metric would call wrong. Its weakness is the opposite one: it measures only what helps pretraining, is insensitive to structure, affordances and provenance entirely, and requires a training run per comparison, so it cannot be used as a per-page check. The convergence is what carries weight: three unrelated methods place Resiliparse in the same band, which is more than can be said for any other tool here.
evidence_independence: Mixed, and the mix runs in Resiliparse's favour in a way worth stating precisely. SIGIR 2023 is author-run -- Bevendorff and Stein are the Webis group that wrote Resiliparse, evaluating Resiliparse -- and must be discounted accordingly. WCXB is NOT: it was built by Murrough Foley, whose own rs-trafilatura tops it, so WCXB has an interest in beating Resiliparse and still ranks it third and above Trafilatura. A favourable placement in a competitor's benchmark is the one form of evidence in this space that is not laundering. DCLM is run by the DataComp-LM consortium, which has no stake in any extractor and selected Resiliparse on measured downstream results plus throughput. Note also a telling absence: Trafilatura's own published evaluation table lists magic-html, jusText, news-please, readability-lxml and goose3 -- and does not include Resiliparse at all, while WCXB places Resiliparse above Trafilatura. The two most-cited author-run benchmarks in this space avoid each other's tools. Conclusion: Resiliparse's approximate standing (competitive with Trafilatura, higher recall, lower precision, much faster) is the single best-corroborated claim in this batch; its exact figures are still corpus-dependent.
page_archetype_coverage: Not reported per type in the sources I could verify -- WCXB publishes per-type breakdowns for rs-trafilatura and Trafilatura but I could not retrieve a full per-type row for Resiliparse, so its 0.797 aggregate is [uncertain] as a per-archetype guide. What can be said structurally: its main_content rule set is boilerplate-removal rather than article-detection, so unlike Readability it does not refuse non-article pages, and unlike rs-trafilatura it does not branch on a predicted page type -- it applies one policy everywhere. That should compress the archetype spread relative to both (less catastrophic on listings, less exceptional on articles), and its high-recall/low-precision profile is consistent with that: on a listing or a collection it will over-collect rather than return nothing. Independently, DCLM's own qualitative finding is that it is particularly effective on table-rich Common Crawl pages, and separately that it loses code-block delimiters and mathematical formatting -- so its weak archetypes are documentation and technical content, exactly where structure is the payload.
script_and_locale_behaviour: The best-positioned of the rule-based tools, because encoding and script handling are a first-class subsystem rather than an afterthought: the Parsing Utilities include dedicated, optimized encoding-detection and normalization tooling, built because Common Crawl is full of mislabelled and broken encodings. Lexbor underneath is a spec-compliant HTML5 parser, so its tokenization does not degrade on non-Latin scripts. The boilerplate rules in main_content mode are still keyed on English structural conventions and will lose their negative half on sites whose class names are non-Latin, and the ASCII formatting mode's line-and-indent conventions assume left-to-right text, so RTL output is emitted without bidi isolation and can render reordered. Whitespace-free segmentation (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) is not addressed: the tool emits text nodes as-is and any downstream length or token heuristic inherits the CJK undercount problem. Net: script-robust at the parse layer, not script-invariant at the extract layer.
leaks_outward: Nothing. No network access in the extraction path, no telemetry, no phone-home, no model download, no analytics. It is a pure function over bytes already in hand, and it does not even ship a fetcher -- unlike Trafilatura's CLI, there is no crawler mode in the extraction library, so there is no second-fetch disclosure risk to inherit. FastWARC in the same repository reads archives from disk or a stream. Of everything in this batch, this is the cleanest disclosure posture.
mechanism_detectability: Zero client-side and zero server-side, in the strongest sense available. It never runs in the page, never patches a DOM API, never touches attachShadow, opens no CDP session, installs no extension, and introduces no timing side channel because it is not present while the page is live. It is not merely undetectable -- it is absent. The corollary is that it contributes nothing to the detectability problem and also nothing to solving it: whatever produced the HTML it consumes owns the entire detectability question. For this project that means Resiliparse is safe to place downstream of the capture and irrelevant to the capture itself.
countermeasures: None needed and none offered, in the privacy direction. The Process Guards subsystem is the closest thing to hardening but it defends the PROCESSOR, not the reader: it enforces execution-time and memory limits on individual tasks so a pathological input cannot hang or OOM a batch job, allowing the task to be skipped or rescheduled. That is availability hardening against adversarial input, and it is a legitimately rare and valuable mechanism -- most extractors in this batch have no answer at all to a zip-bomb-shaped DOM. Against sites defending themselves, the usual asymmetry applies: client-side rendering defeats it entirely, and it has no fallback because it has no browser.
measured_fidelity_cost: Measured better than any peer on one axis and not at all on the others. The recall/contamination pair against WCXB's ground truth is an explicit, decomposed fidelity statement -- 74.5% content retained, 22.8% boilerplate admitted -- with the control being a curated span rather than the full capture, so it still does not answer 'how much of what was there survived'. DCLM's swap-the-extractor-and-retrain design is the only measurement in this batch with a real control (WET files as baseline, +2.5 Core points), and it is a downstream-utility cost rather than a fidelity cost. Nothing measures affordance retention: with form_fields and links on, some fraction of controls appears as text, and that fraction has never been computed -- which is a direct, cheap, and currently unclaimed experiment against this project's 80.9%-of-99.7% figure. No measurement anywhere frames loss as the cost of a hardening decision, because there is no hardening decision to cost.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded and not representable, with one structural mitigation: because Resiliparse is normally fed from WARC archives, the gate state MAY be recoverable from the WARC record's HTTP status, headers and Set-Cookie fields even though Resiliparse itself neither reads nor propagates it. That is a property of the container format, not of the extractor, and it is exactly why pairing extraction with WARC-style capture metadata is the right architecture. Within the extractor there is no consent-banner field, no paywall flag, no login state, no CAPTCHA marker; a consent overlay's copy is discarded if its container matches a boilerplate rule and silently kept as content if it does not. With roughly two-thirds of top sites presenting a consent interface, every corpus built by feeding Resiliparse raw HTML rather than WARC records silently mixes gated and ungated captures.
determinism: Deterministic within a pinned version: pure computation over a Lexbor DOM, no randomness, no clock, no network, no model artifact, no learned component anywhere in the path. There is no cross-call cached state (contrast Trafilatura's deduplication LRU), so repeated extraction of the same document in one process is idempotent. The one caveat is the Process Guards: if a guard is armed and a task exceeds its time or memory limit, that task is aborted or skipped, so under resource pressure the same input can produce output on one run and nothing on another -- non-determinism introduced deliberately at the availability boundary. That is the right tradeoff and it fails loudly, but it must be accounted for in any reproducibility claim.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts on two axes, both narrower than its peers'. The boilerplate rule set in main_content mode is revised between releases, so main_content output moves; the visible-text serializer path (main_content=False) is far more stable because it is essentially 'walk the DOM and emit text', which is closer to a specification than a heuristic. The second axis is Lexbor: an HTML5-spec parser upgrade changes tree construction on malformed input (implied elements, foster parenting, encoding sniffing), so the same bytes through two Lexbor versions are not the same tree. Because Lexbor targets the WHATWG spec rather than a house style, this drift is toward the standard rather than randomly, which is a meaningfully better position than lxml/libxml2's. Pin (resiliparse version, lexbor version) and record both.
reproducibility: Strong at the tool layer and unusually strong at the evidence layer. The SIGIR 2023 study is a reproducibility study by construction, with code and unified datasets published under Apache-2.0 in chatnoir-eu/web-content-extraction-benchmark including the model outputs, so its ranking can be re-run rather than merely cited -- that is the discipline this space mostly lacks. WCXB likewise publishes HTML, ground truth and baseline outputs. DCLM's result is reproducible only at the cost of a pretraining run, so in practice it is a one-time finding. What none of them reproduces is the live web: all corpora are frozen. The mirror-image warning for this project stands -- frozen corpora go stale, live-refetching corpora are not corpora, and the only defensible answer is a pinned capture set plus a separately-tracked live refresh, which is precisely what the WARC pairing enables.
failure_modes: (1) SPA yields shell -- silent, and the dominant modern failure. (2) main_content mode over-collects: its 22.8% boilerplate admission means navigation and sidebar text routinely lands in the output, so downstream consumers see contaminated content rather than missing content. This is the inverse of Readability's failure and is much easier to detect and to repair downstream, which is an underrated property. (3) Structural markers lost even when text survives: markdown code-fence delimiters dropped so code becomes indistinguishable from prose, and mathematical formatting stripped to bare textual components -- documented as a specific weakness against Trafilatura's different specific weakness (Trafilatura discards math entirely and strips code indentation). Neither tool is right; they are wrong in complementary directions. (4) Resource exhaustion on pathological input, converted by Process Guards into an explicit abort. (5) Encoding misdetection on undeclared charsets, mitigated but not eliminated by the encoding subsystem. (6) Shadow content silently absent with no marker.
failure_visibility: Better than its peers on one failure and no better on the rest. The Process Guard mechanism is genuine loud failure: a task that exceeds time or memory is aborted, reported and reschedulable rather than silently producing truncated garbage, and that is the single most transferable reliability idea in this item. Everything else degrades silently -- there is no confidence score (contrast rs-trafilatura's quality predictor), no field naming which rules fired, no count of removed containers, no marker for unreachable content. Its high-recall bias makes silent failure less dangerous in practice than a high-precision tool's: over-collection is visible to a downstream reader in a way that quiet deletion is not, so the failure that dominates is at least in principle detectable. That is a mitigation, not a mechanism.
scale_limits: The best in this batch by a wide margin, and it is the reason DCLM chose it: roughly 8x faster than Trafilatura on the same workload, with parsing throughput on the order of 1,150 documents/second, achieved by doing the work in C on a Lexbor tree with no Python object graph in the hot path. Cost is linear in document size with a very small constant; there is no fallback cascade to trigger a multi-pass worst case. It is still whole-document in memory with no streaming at the document level, so cost tracks total DOM size rather than kept-content size, and a chrome-heavy page costs the same as a prose-heavy one. Where linearity actually stops is memory on pathological documents, and that boundary is the one place in this batch where a tool has an explicit, configurable answer instead of an OOM.
delta_cost_model: None, and structurally impossible in its current form. Every call re-parses the entire document into a fresh Lexbor tree and re-walks it; a one-character change costs a full re-run. Every change class is outside any bound: text edits, attribute changes, subtree insertion, CSS-driven change (invisible), canvas (invisible), shadow mutations (invisible), and declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse -- which Lexbor as a spec-compliant HTML5 parser will handle according to whatever the current specification says, meaning behaviour here is version-dependent and worth an explicit test rather than an assumption. [uncertain] on exactly how the installed Lexbor version treats declarative shadow DOM templates. Its saving grace is the constant factor: at ~1,150 docs/s a whole-page re-run is cheap enough that the O(page) cost may be tolerable in an actuator-layer role even though it can never satisfy o_delta as a fold.
reanchoring_stability: No node identity, no re-anchoring, no measurable re-anchor rate. The output carries no xpath, no source offsets, no element ids, no content hashes; even 'minimal_html' mode preserves element TYPE, not element IDENTITY. Two runs across a page version can only be compared by text diff, which conflates a DOM move with a content edit. It does not even carry the document url that Trafilatura's TEI header provides -- the caller supplies and tracks that. Against W3C Web Annotation dual selectors or content-defined-chunking boundaries it sits at the floor, and the gap is total: address is exactly the thing this tool discards to go fast.
adversarial_exposure: Exposed, with one meaningful default in its favour and one meaningful hazard against it. In its favour: `hidden_elements` defaults to EXCLUDED, so attribute-level concealment (inline display:none, visibility:hidden, the hidden attribute, aria-hidden) is filtered by default rather than by caller diligence -- and the toggle makes the policy explicit and auditable, which is better than an implicit rule buried in a scorer. Against it: it cannot read computed style, so stylesheet-class concealment, off-screen positioning, zero-height clipping, zero font-size and background-matched colour all pass straight through, and unlike Readability it has no deletion-volume accident to protect it -- its high-recall bias means it keeps MORE of the page, so a concealed payload anywhere on the page is more likely to survive Resiliparse than any high-precision extractor. That is the structural point for this project: a recall-first, layout-blind reader is the most exposed configuration there is, and it is also the configuration this project has chosen. Additional specific hazards: `alt_texts` is on by default (attacker-controlled text with no visual counterpart, a classic injection channel), `noscript` content can be surfaced, and `form_fields` emits placeholder text, which is likewise attacker-controlled and never seen by a human who does not focus the field.
provenance_carrying: None at any granularity from the extractor itself -- not per token, not per element, not per document. No url, no xpath, no capture timestamp, no shadow depth, no gate state. Everything must be carried by the container. This is why the FastWARC pairing in the same repository is the architecturally interesting part: a WARC record carries target URI, capture timestamp, request and response headers, and a record ID, so the document-level half of provenance exists one layer out even though the extractor throws it away. The lesson is negative and useful: co-locating a fast extractor with an archive format does not give you per-token provenance, it gives you per-record provenance and a hard join problem, because nothing connects an output token back to a source offset. This project's url:xpath:markdown:content key supplies for free the exact join that the Resiliparse/FastWARC pairing cannot make.
roundtrip_safety: Not a fixed point in any mode. Feeding plain-text output back in yields the text again only trivially (it is no longer HTML); feeding 'minimal_html' output back in yields a different, smaller result because the boilerplate rules have lost the class and container signals they keyed on. The escaping policy is the weak spot in the formatted modes: ASCII formatting inserts bullets, indentation and blank lines as structure-bearing characters with no escaping of source text that already contains them, so a source line beginning with a bullet character or a source paragraph containing the indentation pattern is indistinguishable from emitted structure -- a straightforward structure-injection channel and a straightforward round-trip failure. 'minimal_html' is closer to safe because structure is markup rather than convention. There is no security-grade sanitization claim anywhere. A fixed-point test over the minimal_html mode is a cheap oracle-free fidelity metric that nobody publishes for this tool.
token_budget_and_ordering: No budget, no truncation policy, no ranking, no ordering contract -- output is document order and the caller owns everything downstream. What it does have, uniquely, is a coarse but honest COST DIAL made of orthogonal switches: turning off alt_texts, links, form_fields, comments, post_meta and list_bullets each removes a nameable category of tokens, and preserve_formatting trades layout tokens against compactness. That is a better budget primitive than Trafilatura's favor_precision/favor_recall because the axes are semantic and independent rather than a single aggressiveness scalar -- a caller can decide to spend tokens on affordances and not on comments. Against the 50%-context-fill position-bias problem it offers nothing: the high-value material lands wherever the page author put it, and past the recency-dominance threshold that is uncontrolled. The transferable idea is the orthogonal-switch design, not any policy it implements.
representation_cost: Roughly 90-97% reduction against source HTML bytes in main_content mode, with the plain-text non-main-content mode landing higher because it keeps all visible text. The formatting modes cost real tokens: ASCII formatting adds blank lines, indentation and bullets, plausibly 10-25% over compact output, and buys recoverable nesting -- that is the same trade this project's ASCII wireframe makes and is worth measuring directly rather than assuming. What is bought per token saved is the usual total loss on the axes that matter here: all interactive STATE, all addressability, all shadow content, all provenance -- but notably NOT all affordance presence, since links and form values survive as text. It is the only tool in this batch where the compression is not purely by deletion of the interactive surface.
what_could_be_adopted: Four mechanisms, and this is the highest-yield item in the extraction half of this batch. (1) The ORTHOGONAL TOGGLE SURFACE -- alt_texts / links / form_fields / noscript / comments / post_meta / list_bullets / hidden_elements / preserve_formatting as independent, caller-set, semantically-named switches. This is directly adoptable as the fold's output policy interface, it is structure-agnostic (every switch names a tag or an attribute class, never a page region), and it turns keep/discard from a baked opinion into a recorded parameter -- which also makes captures comparable, because the switch settings can be stored with the artifact. (2) `preserve_formatting=True` as prior art for the ASCII-wireframe rendering: it is an existing, battle-tested convention for encoding nesting and list structure in plain text at Common-Crawl scale, and its escaping gap (source text containing bullets or indentation is indistinguishable from emitted structure) is a bug this project should fix rather than reproduce. (3) PROCESS GUARDS: time and memory limits per unit of work, with the excess converted into an explicit abort-and-reschedule rather than a hang or an OOM. This is the loud-failure mechanism the project's no-mocks/loud-failure posture already wants and does not have, and it is applicable to per-node folding as directly as to per-document extraction. (4) `main_content=False` as the baseline extractor: the visible-text serializer with no boilerplate rules at all is the structure-agnostic control this project should be measuring against, and it is available for free inside a tool everyone benchmarks only in its other mode. What must NOT be adopted: the main_content rule set itself.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: SPLIT VERDICT, and this is the one tool in the batch where the split is real. With main_content=True -- REJECTED: the rule set removes navigation, sidebars and footers, which is a region classifier by any reading. With main_content=False -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS: the visible-text serializer applies only tag-level rules (skip script/style/template) and attribute-level visibility checks, names no region, and encodes no page-structure prior. The toggle is the constraint boundary, and the compliant mode is the one nobody benchmarks. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. No geometry, no rendering, no computed style; the hidden-element predicate is attribute-local. o_delta: REJECTED as a fold. Whole-document re-parse per call, every change class outside any bound, shadow and CSS changes invisible. Mitigated but not cured by a very small constant factor (~1,150 docs/s), which makes it viable in the actuator layer where a whole-page re-run is affordable. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and positively so -- no learned component, no model artifact, no stub surface anywhere in the measured path, and Process Guards convert resource failure into an explicit signal rather than a silent truncation. It is the most no-mocks-compatible tool in the batch. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY. It never touches attachShadow so it cannot violate the rule, but it also never traverses open shadow roots and emits no unreachable marker, so it silently under-reports shadow content and would benchmark well while missing entire components -- the dishonest-coverage pattern the constraint exists to prevent. OVERALL VERDICT: ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY as a component, with the toggle surface, the ASCII formatting convention, the process-guard mechanism, and the main_content=False baseline all extractable as-is into the fold's design.
governance_signal_handling: None, and cleanly none: the extraction library has no fetcher at all, so there is no robots.txt path, no Content Signals parsing, no ai.txt, no IETF AIPREF vocabulary, no Web Bot Auth signature or Signature Agent Card, and no HTTP 402 handling. Every governance obligation belongs to whatever produced the WARC or the HTML. This is architecturally the right separation -- the reader should not be the fetcher -- but it means adopting Resiliparse contributes nothing to a governance story and cannot be cited as compliance. One indirect point: because the canonical input is a WARC record, the fetch-time governance context (status codes, response headers, robots decisions if recorded) is at least available adjacent to the content, which is more than a raw-HTML pipeline can say.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The library retains nothing; the caller's persisted artifact is the regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026. What it hands you is PII-rich by default and in a specific way worth flagging: `comments` and `post_meta` are ON by default, so user-generated content and author metadata are included unless the caller explicitly opts out -- the inverse of the defensible default, and the opposite of Trafilatura's include_comments=False. `form_fields=True` additionally surfaces input VALUES, which on a captured page can include text a user typed: search queries, partially-completed forms, and in the worst case credentials or personal details present in the DOM at capture time. That is a materially different and more sensitive category than published page text, it is invisible to anyone reading the output as prose, and no consumer of this tool appears to discuss it. Any adoption of the form_fields idea in this project must treat captured input values as a distinct, more-restricted class rather than as page content. No gate-state marker and no capture timestamp are emitted, so a legitimate-interest balancing test over a Resiliparse-built store has nothing to work from unless the WARC layer supplies it. [uncertain] on the precise EDPB 03/2026 treatment of incidentally-captured form input values, which I could not verify against the guidance text.
